en.title: BridgePulse: Bridge Damage Classification
en.summary: A signal-processing and ML research pipeline that classifies experimental bridge damage from acceleration recordings, with state-grouped evaluation and a standalone prediction package.
en.goal: Can vibration measurements distinguish baseline and experimentally damaged bridge states while keeping recordings from the same state out of both sides of a validation split?
approach: Read H5 acceleration recordings from 29 sensors and 58 channels at 128 Hz, validating channel presence, signal length and finite values.
Use a fixed 89-second segment, overlapping 4-second windows and eight MFCCs per channel to extract 1,392 features using median, interquartile range and mean absolute change.
Evaluate a regularized Random Forest with experimental states kept together in every split; package feature extraction, a pretrained model, CLI prediction and JSON output.
Include a model card, locked research dependencies, audit reports and scripts for optional local MLflow registration.
observations: The saved final pipeline audit reports mean balanced accuracy of 81.97%, with a standard deviation of 8.14 percentage points across state-grouped allocations.
The repository provides a standalone prediction package and a bundled model; prediction does not require retraining or MLflow.
limitations: The dataset contains 25 recordings from eight experimental states on one bridge. Features and parameters were selected through exploration, with no untouched final test set.
The bundled model is trained on all 25 recordings; predictions on those recordings do not measure generalization. Reported scores are not calibrated probabilities.
This classifies an experimental condition, rather than forecasting future cracks, and has not been validated for bridge safety decisions.
The source H5 dataset is not bundled. Results are cited from saved reports; the pipeline was not rerun for this portfolio review.
credits: MFCC extraction and classification use established signal-processing and scikit-learn tools.

en.title: JEV: Structured AI Decision Experiments
en.summary: A Python experimentation suite evaluating constrained model decisions in flight, driving, chess and a custom reasoning exam, with saved traces, comparisons and deterministic flight replay.
en.goal: How do structured telemetry, explicit action choices and prompt revisions affect model decisions across simulated environments and reasoning tasks?
approach: Integrate typesafe/jev-1.13 through OpenRouter with structured state inputs and explicitly defined actions or answers.
Build a PyFlyt flight experiment comparing one policy selecting joint pitch/bank actions with two policies dividing the axes, then iterate on numerical guidance and a 45-action space.
Compare highway driving with DQN policies, chess decisions with Maia and Stockfish, and answer choices on a custom 50-question knowledge and reasoning exam.
Preserve decisions, outcomes and evaluation reports, and support local flight replay from recorded episodes without further model calls.
observations: The saved v8 flight report records completion of all eight frames on seeds 44, 45 and 46 after prompt revisions. These were three previously tested seeds.
The repository includes a 32-flight matched navigation evaluation, chess and driving comparisons, exam outputs and recorded flight videos.
limitations: Flight and driving are simulations. Small exploratory samples on reused seeds do not establish reliability on new courses or real-world control.
The custom exam has not been calibrated with human participants; results are task-specific rather than a general intelligence benchmark.
Live model runs require OpenRouter access and credits. Large videos and engines use Git LFS, and bundled chess executables target Windows.
The portfolio cites saved source artifacts; live simulations and API-backed evaluations were not rerun during this review.
credits: Uses the existing JEV model and OpenRouter API, PyFlyt for flight simulation, and Maia/Stockfish as chess opponents.

en.title: Speech Emotion Recognition with MFCCs
en.summary: An audio classification experiment turning speech recordings into MFCC features for a Random Forest emotion classifier.
en.goal: Explore an audio preprocessing and classification pipeline, from waveform input to an emotion label.
approach: Remove silence, normalize recordings and average 30 MFCC coefficients per sample.
Encode labels and train a Random Forest using TESS speech recordings; save processing and model artifacts.
observations: The notebook records 2,800 audio samples and includes saved classification output and recording/inference code.
limitations: The evaluation uses a random file split and does not establish performance on unseen speakers.
Emotion names include inconsistent case and wording. Labels should be normalized before treating the evaluation as a stable result.
The microphone inference cell omits the StandardScaler transformation used during training; that path needs correction before reliable live use.
credits: The audio data is identified as the Toronto Emotional Speech Set (TESS).
